R01.text: For most of the recent 14 days, your metrics matched your 28-day baseline: sleep near 7.8 hours (starting ~22:50, ending 07:00), steps ~8,000, active minutes ~55, and resting heart rate ~56 bpm. However, on April 3-6, your resting heart rate rose to 65-67 bpm (baseline 55-57) and HRV dropped to 23-26 ms (baseline 43-47). Both returned to baseline levels by April 7. Sleep, steps, and activity did not change during those four days. This isolated multi-day deviation resolved fully.

R03.text: Your sleep stayed stable near your 28-day baseline of ~470 min, consistently ending at 07:00 with starts around 22:45–22:58. Steps (~8,000) and active minutes (~55) were unchanged. A notable shift occurred Apr 3–6: resting heart rate rose from your typical 55–57 bpm to 65–67 bpm while RMSSD dropped from ~45 ms to 23–26 ms. Both returned to baseline by Apr 7. This four-day cluster was isolated; no corresponding change in sleep or activity was observed. In the window, RHR and RMSSD became strongly inversely correlated (r≈−0.97), unlike baseline (r≈0.13). Continue monitoring to see if such episodes recur.

R04.text: Sleep duration (~470 min), timing (onset ~22:50, offset 07:00), steps (~8043 vs ~7996), activity (~55 min), and low movement (~451 vs ~447 min) remained stable across the 28-day baseline and 14-day window. However, on window days 4–7 (Apr 3–6), resting HR rose from a baseline of 55–57 bpm to 65–67 bpm while RMSSD dropped from 43–47 ms to 23–26 ms; both returned to baseline ranges by Apr 7. This transient deviation drove window variance increases. During the window, same-day resting HR and RMSSD correlated strongly negatively (r=−0.97), unlike baseline (r=0.13).

R07.text: Over 28 days baseline then 14 days window, sleep duration (~470 min), steps (~8000), activity (~55 min), and low movement (~451 min) remained stable with consistent sleep timing (start ~22:50, end 07:00). Resting heart rate rose from a tight 55-57 bpm baseline to 65-67 bpm on window days 5-8 before returning to 55-57 bpm. HRV RMSSD concurrently dropped from 43-47 ms to 23-26 ms during the same four-day interval, recovering to 44-47 ms thereafter. Window RHR-HRV correlation was strongly inverse (r=-0.97) versus weak at baseline (r=0.13). Daytime wear was complete throughout.

R09.text: Across the 28-day baseline, sleep averaged 470 min (~22:50-07:00), steps ~8043, activity ~55 min, low movement ~451 min, RHR 56 bpm, and RMSSD 45 ms. During the 14-day window, sleep (+1 min), steps (-47), activity (+0.4 min), and low movement (-4 min) remained near baseline. However, RHR rose by 2.7 bpm and RMSSD fell by 6.1 ms, driven by a distinct four-day episode (Apr 3-6) where RHR reached 65-67 bpm and RMSSD dropped to 23-26 ms before returning to baseline levels (RHR 55-56, RMSSD 44-47) for the remaining ten days. This transient shift produced a strong inverse RHR-RMSSD correlation in the window (r=-0.97) absent at baseline (r=0.13). Daytime structure and sleep timing were unchanged throughout.

audit.audit_limitations: This audit is a provisional LLM analysis of synthetic wearable data against anonymous text representations. It cannot establish clinical truth, diagnose conditions, or determine causation for the observed RHR/HRV deviations. The PROVISIONAL_LLM_GOLD labels are fallible relevance indicators, not human ground truth. No representations were assumed superior. All interpretations of 'spontaneous' resolution or 'autonomic' changes are flagged as unsupported because the raw data lacks causal, symptomatic, or clinical context. The arithmetic seeds are generic calculations applied uniformly and do not imply diagnostic significance. This audit itself cannot serve as a final research conclusion.
